questions.question: For P(−3; 1) and Q(5; −5), calculate the distance PQ, the midpoint of PQ, and the gradient of PQ, explaining what each formula is really doing.
questions.expected_answer: Distance: the horizontal change is 5 − (−3) = 8 and the vertical change is −5 − 1 = −6 (size 6); these are the legs of a right-angled triangle with PQ as hypotenuse, so PQ = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 — the distance formula is Pythagoras written in coordinates. Midpoint: average each coordinate separately, ((−3 + 5)/2; (1 + (−5))/2) = (1; −2) — both coordinates must be averaged, not just one. Gradient: change in y over change in x with a consistent subtraction order top and bottom: (−5 − 1)/(5 − (−3)) = −6/8 = −3/4 — negative, so the line falls from left to right, which a rough sketch confirms.

questions.question: Find the equation of the line through (4; 1) perpendicular to y = 4x − 7, and explain the perpendicular gradient rule including the pair of lines it cannot handle.
questions.expected_answer: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so invert the given gradient and reverse its sign: from 4 to −1/4 (check: 4 × (−1/4) = −1). Substitute the point into y = mx + c: 1 = (−1/4)(4) + c, so 1 = −1 + c, giving c = 2. The line is y = −1/4 x + 2. The invert-and-reverse rule is a quarter turn of the gradient triangle: run and rise swap roles and the direction of climb reverses. The rule cannot handle the horizontal-vertical pair: a horizontal line has gradient 0 and a vertical line has no gradient, so the product −1 cannot be formed — their perpendicularity is stated geometrically instead.

questions.question: Define the inclination of a line, find it for gradients 1 and −3/4, and explain why the calculator's raw answer for the negative gradient must be adjusted.
questions.expected_answer: The inclination θ is the angle the line makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise, with 0° ≤ θ < 180°, and it satisfies m = tan θ. For m = 1: θ = tan⁻¹(1) = 45°, acute because the line rises. For m = −3/4 the line falls, so θ must be obtuse — tangent is negative between 90° and 180°. Work with the size: tan⁻¹(3/4) = 36,87° is the reference angle, so θ = 180° − 36,87° = 143,13°. Typing −3/4 into inverse tan returns −36,87°, an angle measured clockwise below the axis; it describes the same line direction (tangent repeats every 180°) but falls outside the defined range for inclination, so it cannot stand as the answer.
